CausalChain: Gut microbiota converts primary bile acids into LCA -> Nanotechnology-enhanced formulation increases local LCA concentration in breast tumors -> LCA binds and activates TGR5 on tumor-associated macrophages -> Activation triggers a refined cAMP/PKA signaling cascade that, in synergy with low-dose LXA4 analogs, modulates NF-κB activity -> This modulation reprograms TAMs from an M2 (tumor-promoting) state to an enhanced M1 (tumor-suppressing) phenotype -> M1 repolarization increases immune surveillance and promotes tumor cell apoptosis -> Augmented antitumor immunity improves chemotherapeutic efficacy, as measured by high-resolution omics
Hypothesis: We hypothesize that a dual-delivery system using nanotechnology can precisely elevate LCA concentrations within the breast tumor microenvironment to robustly activate TGR5 on tumor-associated macrophages. This activation initiates a refined cAMP/PKA signaling cascade, which, when combined with low doses of LXA4 analogs to support anti-inflammatory signaling, effectively shifts TAMs from an immunosuppressive M2 phenotype to an immunostimulatory M1 phenotype. This reprogramming enhances local immune surveillance and tumor cell apoptosis, ultimately improving the efficacy of chemotherapeutic regimens. This hypothesis will be rigorously tested via integrated high-resolution omics alongside detailed pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic assessments to validate each mechanistic step and ensure specificity of the nanodelivery system.
Abstract: In this study, we propose an advanced therapeutic strategy that leverages nanotechnology-enabled delivery of lithocholic acid (LCA) to reprogram tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs) within breast tumor microenvironments. Building on our original hypothesis that LCA, at physiological levels, activates the TGR5 receptor on TAMs to induce a cAMP/PKA signaling cascade modulating NF-κB activity and thereby shifting macrophages from an M2 immunosuppressive to an M1 immunostimulatory phenotype, we now integrate refinements informed by recent evidence. Specifically, we address criticisms regarding the sufficiency of LCA in effecting this change and potential off-target effects by proposing a dual-modulatory approach that co-delivers low-dose pro-resolving mediators (e.g., lipoxin A4 analogs) alongside LCA. This approach not only targets TGR5 activation but also leverages complementary receptor-mediated pathways, increasing specificity and synergy in macrophage reprogramming. Our advanced nanodelivery system is engineered with high target specificity, controlled release kinetics, and conjugated imaging agents for real-time tracking. The entire cascade—from nanotechnology-assisted accumulation in the tumor microenvironment to a precisely controlled modulation of the cAMP/PKA–NF-κB axis—is designed to be validated through integrated high-resolution omics platforms and rigorous in vitro/in vivo models, ensuring a comprehensive and robust dissection of the molecular interplay underlying enhanced tumor immune surveillance, apoptosis, and chemotherapeutic responses.
Orignal_vs_New: The original hypothesis proposed that nanotechnology-enabled delivery of LCA can trigger TGR5-mediated macrophage reprogramming via the cAMP/PKA–NF-κB cascade to improve antitumor immunity and chemotherapy response. In the revised hypothesis, we have directly addressed critiques by: (1) incorporating an additional co-delivery of a low-dose LXA4 analog to enhance specificity and synergize anti-inflammatory actions, thereby mitigating off-target effects and strengthening the mechanistic plausibility; (2) refining the nanotechnology aspect by including features such as controlled release and real-time imaging; (3) detailing a more rigorous validation strategy using integrated high-resolution omics platforms and pharmacological measurements; and (4) explicitly delineating each step of the causal chain to maintain logical coherence and practicality. These enhancements increase the novelty, scientific rigor, and practical implementability of the original concept.
